# Amalgamation Timing & Successive Refinement — Research Findings
**Date:** 2026-08-06 · **For:** the CW Step-8 walk design (PEDAGOGY §29 — append → amalgamate → the
living outline moves forward). Commissioned by Neil in-session (*"you might wanna do a bit of
research on that… spawn some subagents"*). Two Opus agents, distinct lenses; returns verbatim below,
synthesis at the end.

**The question:** the walk appends new lens-material under each beat; the student then AMALGAMATES
it into one improved beat. Does amalgamation happen (a) per-beat, immediately; (b) batched per stage
(~6 beats); (c) delayed to a later session? Neil's prior: (a), *"while the new material is still
fresh."*

---

## PART 1 — Successive-refinement project shape (agent 2, returned first)

### VERDICT
**Qualified yes to the seven-pass shape.** Seven passes is inside the productive range — the only
quantitative plateau found is at ~11 revisions (Wilson et al. 2014), with the bulk of gain in the
first ~5 (Potter & Wilson 2021). Direct support for the shape: students who wrote FEWER pieces and
revised them MANY times gained more than students who wrote many pieces revised less (Huang &
Wilson 2021).

**The biggest risk is NOT fatigue — it is SURFACE DRIFT.** Novice revisers fail to *detect*
occasions for revision and default to word/sentence tinkering rather than global change (Bereiter &
Scardamalia, CDO model). Passes 4–7 silently degrade into cosmetic passes unless each supplies an
explicit external criterion — the lens-per-pass design is exactly the right countermeasure; the
risk is execution. Second risk: participation collapse — in statewide data fewer than a quarter of
students revised even once when revision was available but not structurally compelled (Wilson et
al.).

### FINDINGS (claim · source · measured · applicability)
1. **Revise one artefact many times > many fresh artefacts.** Huang & Wilson (2021), *Computers and
   Composition* 62. AWE usage data, proficiency gains. **Direct.** ⚠️ finding verified via a vendor
   research review, not the primary text.
2. **Gains decelerate, plateau ~11 revisions.** Wilson, Olinghouse & Andrada (2014), *Learning
   Disabilities: A Contemporary Journal* 12. Grades 4–8, >4000 students, HLM. **Direct** — 7 passes
   is pre-plateau.
3. **Most improvement within the first five revisions.** Potter & Wilson (2021), *ETR&D* 69(3).
   Grades 4–11, two years of Utah Compose. **Direct** — passes 6–7 must be cheap or carry genuinely
   new content.
4. **Novices under-detect problems; they edit rather than revise.** Bereiter & Scardamalia CDO
   (1983/85). **Analogous→direct.** ⚠️ via secondary reviews.
5. **Explicit strategy instruction (0.82) ≈ 3× study-of-models (0.25).** Graham & Perin (2007),
   *JEP* 99(3), 154 effect sizes. Criteria-first beats example-first. **Direct.**
6. **SRSD 0.84 at grades 6–12** (other strategy instruction 0.51). Graham et al. (2024), *Reading
   and Writing* best-evidence meta-analysis. **Direct.**
7. **Process goals + progress feedback beat product goals.** Schunk & Swartz (1993). N=40 grade 4;
   skill, maintenance, generalisation, self-efficacy. Writers cannot self-gauge progress.
   **Analogous** (younger), mechanism transfers.
8. **Postponed revision → MORE revisions than revising during writing.** Chanquoy (2001), *BJEP*.
   N=60, grades 3–5. **Analogous** — supports the separate-lesson-per-pass structure itself.
9. **Long-project motivation = task focus + perceived competence + value; novelty only starts it.**
   Blumenfeld et al. (1991), *Educational Psychologist* 26. **Analogous.**
10. **Goal-gradient / endowed progress.** Kivetz et al. (2006); Nunes & Drèze (2006). **Lore here**
    (consumer research).

### DESIGN IMPLICATIONS (agent's, kept verbatim in substance)
1. **Every pass opens with a code-served orientation, never a re-read** — the lens, its criteria,
   one-line recap of the outline's current state (findings 4+5).
2. **One lens, explicit criteria, stated BEFORE the artefact appears.** Never "improve with
   archetypes in mind"; always "a strong archetype pass does A, B, C." Highest-leverage rule.
3. **Diff the artefact, don't redisplay it** — highlight what changed since the last pass so
   re-exposure cost falls per pass. ⚠️ labelled INFERENCE (no direct study of change-highlighting
   in student self-revision found).
4. **Progress signal is a PROCESS goal** — "Lens 4 of 7 built in", never "your outline is 57%
   good" (finding 7).
5. **Front-load weight; make passes 6–7 cheap** (finding 3) — genre + structural elements should be
   the shortest passes or they read as repetition, which is what kills long-project motivation
   (finding 9).

### AGENT 2 — COULD NOT VERIFY
Kellogg & Whiteford (2009) full text (no claim drawn) · Thomas (2000) PBL review (unextractable) ·
Berninger (not searched) · optimal pass-count for LENS-DIFFERENTIATED passes (findings 2–3 are from
open-ended AWE revision; lens-per-pass may sustain returns further — plausible extrapolation, NOT
evidenced) · an "engagement declines 75%→33%" figure traced only to blogs — excluded.

## PART 2 — Revision timing per-beat vs per-stage (agent 1, returned second)

### VERDICT
**(a) — immediate, beat-by-beat — with one reframe that dissolves most of the apparent tension.**
All three options are already "delayed" in the sense the revision literature measures: the student
drafted the beat in an EARLIER lesson. Chanquoy's postpone-and-win finding compares
revising-WHILE-composing vs revising-after — it does not license further delay once composing has
ended, and says nothing about batching within a revision session. **The delay benefit is already
banked by the lesson structure regardless of a/b/c.** What remains is a within-session question,
and there the evidence runs the other way: novice adolescents drop to surface edits when revision
load is high, and batching 6 beats maximises load at the moment of 6 substantive judgements.
**Confidence: moderate** (no study directly tests beat-level batching in creative writing).
**Strongest counter-evidence:** Rijlaarsdam & van den Bergh — rereading/goal-setting predict text
quality when they occur in the LAST phase → argues for one whole-stage pass after the per-beat work.

### FINDINGS (claim · source · measured · applicability)
1. **Postponed revision → more revisions AND deeper ones than revision during writing.** Chanquoy
   (2001), *BJEP* 71, 15–41. 60 children, 3 sessions. **Direct** on delay; **analogous** on age
   (8–11 vs our 13–16).
2. **Surface-over-meaning dominance significant ONLY for younger children or during-writing
   revision.** Same source. The discriminator: concurrent revision pins novices to surface edits;
   separated revision lifts the bias. **Direct.**
3. **Novice adolescents default to surface edits without explicit instruction; substantive-revision
   instruction produces the largest gains.** *Behavioral Sciences* 16(1):123 (2026), 88 students
   aged 13–15, four conditions. **Direct** — same age band, same goal.
4. **Procedural facilitation per UNIT increases revision.** Scardamalia & Bereiter CDO — after each
   sentence the child picked one of eleven evaluative prompts; more revisions than untrained;
   ⚠️ quality effects inconsistent across replications. **Direct precedent for immediate per-unit
   revision with a scaffold.**
5. **Resumption cost is real but removed by cues** (Altmann & Trafton memory-for-goals). Timescale
   is seconds-to-minutes; our goal is fully externalised on screen — the exact cueing condition
   that removes the cost. **Analogous.**
6. **Immediate feedback wins in applied classroom studies; delayed wins in lab list-learning.**
   Kulik & Kulik (1988), *RER* 58(1). **Analogous.**
7. **Planning, translating, reviewing compete for one central-executive resource.** Kellogg (2001),
   *AJP* 114 — why concurrent revision fails; one operation at a time. **Analogous.**
8. **For WM-limited learners: keep key information visible, reduce steps** (Gathercole & Alloway
   2008). Keep the new material ADJACENT to the beat; never ask them to hold 6 sets. **Practitioner.**
9. **Interleaving can be an UNdesirable difficulty for low-achieving adolescent novices** (Hwang
   2025, *Language Learning*, L2). Supports repeating the SAME operation across beats. **Weak/
   cross-domain.**
10. **Cool-off/drawer-time before revising: craft LORE only** — no experimental support found for
    multi-day incubation improving adolescent revision.

### THE CHANQUOY DETAIL
60 children, grades 3/4/5. (i) 3rd graders revised MORE; (ii) both postponed conditions beat the
concurrent one on frequency AND depth; (iii) surface bias significant only for younger/during-
writing. ⚠️ **No advantage of the longer postponement over the shorter** — so it does not support
(c) over (b). ⚠️ Exact delay durations unverifiable from the abstract; population is below our band.

### AGENT 1 — COULD NOT VERIFY
Chanquoy's exact delays (full text unreachable) · Fitzgerald (1987) beyond abstract · Faigley &
Witte taxonomy via secondary · Sweller not primary-sourced this session · Kellogg 2001 and
Rijlaarsdam & van den Bergh at abstract level · no MacArthur single citable study (finding 3 rests
on the 2026 study) · no study of interleaving applied to writing revision · King's drawer = lore.

---

## SYNTHESIS — the answer, and it is convergent

**Amalgamation happens PER BEAT, immediately after that beat's new material — Neil's stated
assumption, confirmed, with a sharper reason than freshness.** The two agents arrive independently
at the same three-part shape:

1. **Per-beat, one operation at a time.** The load argument (Kellogg, Gathercole & Alloway), the
   novice surface-drift argument (Bereiter & Scardamalia; the 2026 secondary study), and the CDO
   per-unit precedent all point the same way. Batching 6 beats maximises exactly the load that
   pushes a 14-year-old to cosmetic edits.
2. **Scaffolded, never open.** The ask is compare–diagnose–operate shaped — *"what does the new
   material say this beat should show? where doesn't your version show it? rewrite the beat"* —
   never "improve this." Criteria-first beats models-first ~3× (Graham & Perin 0.82 vs 0.25).
3. **One short whole-stage pass AFTER the six beats** — continuity/contradiction reread only, not a
   re-revision (Rijlaarsdam & van den Bergh last-phase effect). This is the one thing batching
   would have bought, purchased for one extra step.

**The reframe that matters:** the "distance improves revision" tradition is NOT violated — the
distance is already banked, because drafting (Step 6) and amalgamating (Step 8+) are separate
lessons. Chanquoy condemns only revising-while-composing; within the revision session itself,
immediate-per-unit wins.

**Plus the project-shape rules from Part 1** that the walk must obey: code-served orientation each
pass (never a re-read); one lens with explicit criteria before the artefact; diff-don't-redisplay
(inference, labelled); process-goal progress ("Lens 1 of 7 built in"); front-load weight — passes
6–7 (genre, structural elements) must be the SHORTEST.

**Honest limits:** no study tests beat-level batching in creative writing directly (moderate
confidence); the pass-count plateau data comes from open-ended revision, not lens-differentiated
passes; CDO's quality effects were inconsistent even as its revision-frequency effects held.
